questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following terms:

(i) Integration of firms. (2 marks)
(ii) External economies of scale. (2 marks)
(iii) Efficiency of labour. (2 marks)
(iv) Indirect production. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Integration of firms.** Integration is the joining together (by merger, takeover or amalgamation) of two or more firms so that they come under one control and act as a single, larger business. It can be *horizontal* (firms at the same stage of production), *vertical* (firms at different stages of production of the same good) or *conglomerate* (firms in unrelated lines of business).

**(ii) External economies of scale.** These are the cost savings (falling average costs) that benefit **all the firms in an industry** because the industry as a whole has grown or is concentrated in one area, and not because any single firm has become larger. Examples: a pool of skilled workers, good roads and electricity in an industrial zone, and the growth of supplier and repair firms around the industry.

**(iii) Efficiency of labour.** This is the ability of workers to produce a large quantity (or good quality) of output in a given time or at a given cost, that is, the *productivity* of labour. It depends on skill and training, health and nutrition, motivation and pay, the tools and machines used, and working conditions. It is measured by output per worker (or per hour worked).

**(iv) Indirect production.** This is the production of **capital goods** (machines, tools, tractors, fishing nets) which are not wanted for themselves but are used to produce consumer goods later. Resources are first used to make the tool and only afterwards to make the final good, which gives a "roundabout" process. It requires some present consumption to be given up, but it raises future output. It contrasts with direct production, where a person makes a good for his or her own use without the help of such tools.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The following are examples of internal and external economies of scale:

- Marketing economies,
- Organised market,
- Financial economies,
- Ancillary services,
- Risk bearing economies,
- Technical economies.

Classify the following examples into internal and external economies of scale. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Economies of scale are **internal** when they arise from the growth of the individual firm itself, and **external** when they arise from the growth of the whole industry (or its location) and are shared by every firm in it.

| Internal economies of scale (benefit one firm that grows large) | External economies of scale (benefit all firms in the industry) |
|---|---|
| Marketing economies | Organised market |
| Financial economies | Ancillary services |
| Risk bearing economies | |
| Technical economies | |

**Explanation (one line each).**

- **Marketing economies (internal):** a large firm spreads the cost of advertising, packaging and its sales force over a large output and buys raw materials in bulk at a discount, so the cost per unit of selling falls.
- **Financial economies (internal):** a large firm is trusted by banks, can borrow more easily and at a lower rate of interest, and can raise capital by issuing shares to the public.
- **Risk bearing economies (internal):** a large firm spreads risks by producing many products and selling in many markets, so a loss in one line is covered by profits in another.
- **Technical economies (internal):** a large firm can afford big, efficient machines and specialised workers (division of labour), and can use fully equipment that cannot be divided into smaller units.
- **Organised market (external):** the firms of an established industry share well-organised markets, such as commodity markets and auction centres, where buyers and sellers meet, so each firm saves the cost of finding customers.
- **Ancillary services (external):** as an industry grows around a town, supplier, transport, repair, banking and insurance firms settle nearby and serve all producers at lower cost.

questions.enonce_markdown: State and explain THREE (3) advantages of horizontal integration. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Horizontal integration is the merger of firms that produce the **same kind of good at the same stage of production** (for example two bakeries or two soap factories). Its advantages are as follows.

1. **Economies of scale.** The combined firm is larger, so it can buy raw materials in bulk at a discount, use bigger machines, share administration and spread overheads over more output. The average cost of production therefore falls, which allows lower prices or higher profit.
2. **Reduced competition and greater market power.** Two rivals become one, so there is less price-cutting competition and the new firm has a bigger share of the market. It can therefore influence the price more easily and earn more stable profits.
3. **Rationalisation and sharing of resources.** Duplicated branches, depots and offices can be closed, and skills, research, distribution networks and advertising can be pooled. Waste is cut and efficiency rises.

**Conclusion.** Horizontal integration lowers costs and strengthens the firm in its market; its main danger for consumers is that reduced competition may lead to higher prices.
